claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is an example of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
Under rapid cooling, the specified phosphorus-containing alloy normally has partial crystallinity or only limited amorphous regions.
Controlled carbon doping will improve the glass-forming ability of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy relative to the same alloy without carbon.
Controlled carbon doping will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy relative to the undoped alloy.
The beneficial effect of carbon requires an optimal carbon concentration.
The intervention should work under rapid-solidification conditions in which formation of an amorphous phase is otherwise attainable.
Carbon atoms integrate into the alloy matrix and modify its local bonding environment.
Carbon incorporation disrupts long-range atomic order.
Carbon incorporation increases the effective configurational entropy of the alloy.
Carbon alters local atomic interactions through possible covalent-bonding character and atomic-size effects.
The carbon-induced changes in local atomic interactions retard crystal nucleation and growth.
Retarding nucleation and growth raises the effective barrier to crystallization during cooling and stabilizes the already-formed amorphous phase.
Carbon-doped samples will have a larger amorphous phase fraction than otherwise comparable undoped samples.
Carbon-doped samples will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than otherwise comparable undoped samples.
Excessive carbon can cause carbide formation, phase separation, or microstructural inhomogeneity.
At slower cooling rates, carbon doping may not provide a noticeable benefit.
